idiom_name: trait Updatable with List[Updatable].foreach or foldLeft
implementation_notes: Scala spells the hook as a trait - the language documentation notes that traits 'let you specify (abstract) interfaces, as well as concrete implementations' - so trait Updatable { def update(dt: Double): Unit } plus a List[Updatable] walked with foreach is the direct realization, and the functional style reshapes the same pattern into a fold that produces the next world instead of mutating objects in place. What replaces the classic structure: the trait replaces the abstract base class and the immutable collection replaces the entity manager, so no extra machinery is required; Indigo, the frame-driven Scala engine, is the library form where one updateModel/updateViewModel pair runs on every FrameTick rather than per entity. The mutable OO form remains the pragmatic choice in performance-sensitive simulations, where trait dispatch and per-frame allocation dominate.
pitfalls: Immutable collections do not make the entities immutable: mutating objects inside a List while claiming referential transparency is the standard trap - either mutate a mutable collection deliberately or fold to a new world.

With immutable collections mid-walk removal disappears (you rebuild the list), but scala.collection.mutable buffers need filterInPlace/removal after the walk; skipped elements are the same bug as elsewhere.
Trait dispatch is megamorphic in mixed collections, and boxing of Double dt plus Option-heavy code allocates inside the frame loop - specialise or use arrays where the profile demands it.
Frame-driven engines expect the whole frame as a pure function: mixing per-entity mutable updates into an Indigo-style architecture fights the engine, so pick one style per subsystem.
